d.title: Layout is a cost decision, and the only one in this module
d.caption: A prompt cache matches a **prefix**, which turns the order of your sections into a pricing choice — the one place in this module where where a section sits matters more than what it says. Everything static goes in front, in an order that never changes, and everything that varies per request goes behind it. One variable token in front of a 3,000-token static block costs you the whole block.

nodes.label: In an order that never changes
So layout, not wording
nodes.sub: is what this lesson is about

d.title: A zero hit rate is invisible unless you log the field
d.caption: 1.13's incident was a carefully ordered 3,000-token prompt with a hit rate of **zero for months**, because of one timestamp near the front. The reason it lasted months is not that the bug was subtle — it is that nobody logged the one field that would have said so. `cached_tokens` arrives on every response, costs nothing to record, and turns a silent overspend into a graph.

nodes.label: Now it is a graph, not a surprise

d.title: Dynamic examples against a cacheable prefix, and the resolution
d.caption: 2.2 argued for retrieving examples per query; 1.13 argued for a byte-identical prefix. These conflict directly and **the resolution is not to pick one** — it is the last row. A cached core example set carries most of the budget, and a few retrieved examples adapt the tail, so you keep most of the discount and most of the adaptation. The first row is worth naming because it is almost always an accident rather than a decision.
cells: the default; examples at full price
if a fixed set is nearly as good
the middle - and usually the answer

d.title: Eight cost levers, ordered by what they actually move
d.caption: The ordering is the point. Effort spent on row six — trimming words from a prompt — is effort not spent on rows one and two, which are **an order of magnitude larger**. A 20% shorter system prompt on a workload that should have been batched is a rounding error on a bill that could have been halved. And the last row moves nothing at all: streaming changes perceived latency and not one token of cost.

items.label: Streaming
items.sub: zero - same cost, better perceived latency

d.title: Conventions, not capabilities
d.caption: Every modern model can follow an instruction, use a delimiter and return structured output. What differs is **which form of each it saw most during training**, and models are measurably better at the form they saw most. Two rows here are more than convention: Google's million-token context is a different design point rather than a preference, and its per-category safety thresholds introduce a failure mode the others do not have.

d.title: A reasoning model rejects the prompt you spent 2.3 learning to write
d.caption: o1 and o3 are the sharpest break from the usual conventions: **no system prompt, no temperature**, and a `developer` role where `system` used to go. The prompting consequence runs deeper than the API shape — these models are trained to do their own decomposition, so walking them through steps is at best redundant and at worst **constrains a search they would have done better unaided**. The structured chain-of-thought of 2.3 is a technique to drop here, not to port.

nodes.label: It decomposes on its own
nodes.sub: that is what it was trained for

nodes.label: Give it the goal, not the method

d.title: The one convention that does not trade off
d.caption: The honest position: XML tags help on Anthropic models more than elsewhere, and they **do not hurt anywhere**. That makes them a reasonable default for any prompt that has to run on several providers — and it is a rare thing in this lesson, because most conventions are a trade where picking one costs you something on another provider.

d.title: A configurable filter is a failure mode you own
d.caption: Gemini exposes a blocking threshold per harm category, which is genuinely useful — a medical or security application can loosen categories that would otherwise block legitimate content. It also introduces a failure **that does not exist on the other providers**: a response blocked by a threshold *you* configured, returning no content and a reason your code has to read. The cost of the control is that the configuration becomes part of your system's behaviour, and belongs in review and in version control with everything else.

nodes.label: A block from your own setting
nodes.sub: no content, and a reason code

d.title: What to keep portable, and what to specialise
d.caption: The split is clean: **the task specification is portable and the mechanism is not**. Instruction, context, output requirements and field semantics say nothing about a provider and are most of the prompt. The three specialise rows are API shapes that belong in the client layer rather than in prompt text. And the operational version of all this is 1.15's warning — a prompt that appears to port cleanly may be silently losing a parameter, a system-prompt privilege or a safety configuration, and only an evaluation surfaces it.

d.title: Six sections, and only one of them is enforceable
d.caption: Writing the sections out separately is useful mainly because it exposes the right-hand column. **Response format is the only one a mechanism can guarantee**; identity is a prior, boundaries are a preference, and examples — the most effective of the six — enforce nothing at all. A prompt that mixes all six into one paragraph hides that distinction, and the distinction is what tells you which lines need a code-level backstop.
cells: what to decline, what to hide

d.title: In a loop, the system prompt is multiplied by the step count
d.caption: 2.5 measured it: in an agent loop the system prompt and every tool definition are re-sent at each step, so at five steps the static prefix was **90% of all input tokens**. Which makes this the one place where trimming a prompt genuinely pays — doubling the system prompt from 400 to 800 tokens adds 4,000 input tokens over ten steps, and 1,600 adds 12,000. The same trimming on a single-call workload would be the rounding error 2.13 called it.

d.title: Three lines every agent prompt has, and none of them work
d.caption: None of this is a reason to omit the line — a prompt instruction raises the bar and costs almost nothing, and "only answer questions about billing" does genuinely reduce off-topic answers. The point is to know which lines are **defences** and which are **preferences**, because the first kind belongs in a threat model and the second does not. The second row is the sharpest: a model that knew its output was fabricated would not have produced it.

cells.text: it is in the context, so it can be reproduced
a model that knew would not have said it

d.title: Prompt or code, decided by whether anything can check it
d.caption: The rule behind every row: **if a mechanism can enforce it, asking is strictly weaker**. Output shape, a forced first tool, a step limit and authorisation all have mechanisms, so a prompt line is at best a second copy of the requirement and at worst the only copy. Tone and domain knowledge have no mechanism, which is exactly what the prompt is for. The last row is the one with a security consequence — the model has no identity; the request does.
